# Roadmap: p-adic differential equations, rigid cohomology and p-adic weights

**Summary.** This roadmap builds the theory that leads from a linear differential equation near the
boundary of a p-adic disc to finite-dimensional cohomology with Frobenius, traces and weights.
Its local half starts from Laurent series converging on annuli: the Robba ring, its bounded and
integral subrings, the Amice ring and the extended Robba ring, with their topologies, Frobenius
lifts, Bézout property and closed ideals, and Monsky–Washnitzer dagger algebras with their
Frobenius lifts. On these rings it develops differential modules (cyclic vectors, generic and
subsidiary radii, Christol–Dwork, Dwork transfer, the variation of radii, the decomposition by
radii and the differential Swan conductor), Frobenius modules (degree, slope, standard modules,
Dieudonné–Manin over the extended Robba ring, Harder–Narasimhan filtrations, generic and special
slopes), Kedlaya's slope filtration theorem and the p-adic local monodromy theorem with its
logarithmic and finite-étale forms, Tsuzuki's finite monodromy theorem for unit-root modules,
Matsuda's decomposition, the equality of irregularity and Swan conductor, and André's local
monodromy group. Its global half builds frames, tubes, strict neighbourhoods and Berthelot's `j†`
functor; convergent and overconvergent `(F-)`isocrystals with their independence of choices, the
Dwork–Berthelot convergence theorem, the Katz–Crew unit-root correspondence and Étesse's descent;
rigid cohomology with compact and closed supports, Frobenius, the Monsky–Washnitzer comparison,
Gysin isomorphisms, dagger and logarithmic comparisons; Kedlaya's finiteness theorem, cohomological
descent along alterations and proper hypercoverings, the trace map, Poincaré duality and the
Künneth formula, the full faithfulness of restriction to convergent isocrystals, and semistable
reduction. It ends with the Lefschetz trace formula and the rationality of `L`-functions of
overconvergent F-isocrystals, the Christol–Mebkhout and Grothendieck–Ogg–Shafarevich formulas, the
p-adic Fourier transform, Kedlaya's p-adic Weil II with its weight theory, the Dwork, Kummer and
Kloosterman isocrystals, the rigid–crystalline comparison with coefficients, and the rationality,
integrality and `ℓ`-independence of the Weil factors of smooth proper varieties over finite fields,
with the denominator, crystalline-lattice and coefficient-congruence bounds underlying
Kedlaya's and Tuitman's point-counting formulas. The end theorems are Kedlaya's
slope filtration and p-adic local monodromy theorems, the finiteness and Poincaré duality of rigid
cohomology with coefficients, p-adic Weil II, and the equality of crystalline, rigid and `ℓ`-adic
Weil factors.

The layers are:

| Layer | Title | Headline targets |
| --- | --- | --- |
| RD.0 | Coefficient rings and analytic foundations | Laurent and Robba carriers, Frobenius lifts on the Robba ring and on dagger algebras, Kedlaya's analytic rings, the extended Robba ring, Bézout property and closed ideals, valuation p-bases, Arabia's controlled lifting |
| RD.1 | Differential modules, radii and Frobenius slopes | cyclic vectors, generic radius, Christol–Dwork, Dwork transfer, variation of subsidiary radii, differential Swan conductor, Frobenius modules, Dieudonné–Manin over the extended Robba ring, Harder–Narasimhan slopes, `(φ,∇)`-modules, Robba residue duality |
| RD.2 | Local monodromy and ramification | isoclinic descent, Kedlaya's slope filtration theorem, Tsuzuki's theorem, the p-adic local monodromy theorem and its logarithmic form, Matsuda's decomposition, `irregularity = Swan`, André's local monodromy group |
| RD.3 | Frames, convergent and overconvergent coefficients | frames, tubes, strict neighbourhoods, `j†`, overconvergent isocrystals and F-isocrystals, independence of the frame, Dwork–Berthelot convergence, convergent F-isocrystals, Katz–Crew, Étesse's descent |
| RD.4 | Rigid cohomology, supports and comparison maps | rigid cohomology with compact and closed supports, Frobenius, the Monsky–Washnitzer comparison, Gysin isomorphisms, log rigid cohomology with proper support, dagger comparisons, the rigid–crystalline comparison map |
| RD.5 | Finiteness, descent, duality and semistable reduction | finiteness on curves and in general, cohomological descent, the trace map, Poincaré duality, Künneth, full faithfulness, extension across the boundary, semistable reduction, relative convergent cohomology |
| RD.6 | Traces, conductors, Fourier transform and weights | closed-point Frobenius, `L`-functions, Dwork operators, the Lefschetz trace formula, Euler–Poincaré and Grothendieck–Ogg–Shafarevich formulas, the Fourier transform, `ι`-weights and p-adic Weil II, Kloosterman isocrystals |
| RD.7 | Coefficient comparisons and Weil factors | Frobenius on the rigid–crystalline comparison, Ogus's comparison with coefficients, weight separation, Weil factors and their `ℓ`-adic comparison, abelian varieties, denominator and coefficient-congruence bounds, Kloosterman Hodge–Newton bounds |

The layer labels RD.0–RD.7 are the labels other roadmaps cite, and target `RD.k.n` is the `n`-th
target of layer RD.`k`.

## Scope and ownership

**Scope.** The Robba-ring coefficient theory for general complete discretely
valued coefficient fields `K` and general Frobenius lifts `σ` (any `q = p^a`, ramified `K`, residue
fields that need not be perfect where a target allows it); the analytic theory of p-adic
differential equations on discs and annuli; the slope and monodromy theory of `(φ,∇)`-modules;
Berthelot's convergent and overconvergent coefficient categories; rigid cohomology with all its
support variants and comparison maps; finiteness, duality, descent and semistable reduction for
overconvergent F-isocrystals; the trace formula, `L`-functions and p-adic Weil II; and the
comparisons that identify rigid, crystalline and `ℓ`-adic Weil factors over finite fields.

**What it takes from the libraries.** Mathlib supplies Laurent and Hahn series
(`LaurentSeries`, `HahnSeries`, `LaurentSeries.hasseDeriv`), power series with their derivative
and restricted-series predicates and Gauss norms (`PowerSeries.derivative`,
`PowerSeries.IsRestricted`, `PowerSeries.gaussNorm`), derivations, Kähler
differentials, smooth and étale algebras, Witt vectors with their Frobenius, the rank-one
classification of isocrystals over an algebraically closed field (`WittVector.Isocrystal`,
`isocrystal_classification`: only rank one, not Dieudonné–Manin), the reversed characteristic
polynomial `Matrix.charpolyRev`, additive characters (`AddChar`), `WithSeminorms` and
`IsUltrametricDist`. Tau Ceti supplies restricted power series and the one-variable Tate algebra
with Weierstrass preparation, comodule categories with their rigid and symmetric structures and
Tannakian reconstruction from a Hopf algebra (`TauCeti.FGComoduleCat`,
`TauCeti.Tannaka.pointsFunctorIsoTensorAutFunctor`), Galois descent for semilinear
representations, the genus, Riemann–Roch spaces and Weil differentials of function fields, the
trace on short exact sequences (`LinearMap.trace_eq_add_of_exact`) and point counts and Frobenius
traces of elliptic curves over finite fields (`WeierstrassCurve.frobeniusTrace`).
Recognition of an abstract neutral Tannakian category is supplied by
MotivesAndAlgebraicCycles §§6.1–6.3. Its application adapter here identifies the reconstructed
category with Tau Ceti's finite comodules and preserves the specified fibre functor ([§RD.6.64](#rd-6-64)).

**What it takes from TauCetiRoadmap.** AdicSpaces for the analytic vocabulary; AlgebraicCurves
Layer 9 for the comparison of Kähler and Weil differentials with residues; EllipticCurves Layer 3
for the criterion "supersingular if and only if `p` divides the trace"; JacobianChallenge Layer `F`
for Jacobians and the Abel–Jacobi map; NewtonPolygons §§2.1, 3.2–3.3 for coefficient polygons,
polynomial products and root multisets; ReductiveGroups Layers 1–3 for Lie algebras of algebraic
groups; LocalFieldsRamification Layers 3–4 for finite and absolute ramification over every
perfect residue field, Herbrand functions, subgroup and quotient compatibility and Hasse–Arf,
using the pinned Tau Ceti Herbrand and upper-numbering API on the finite-residue-field domain; and EtaleCohomologyFoundations §`F`.0.2 for étale fundamental groups and
InverseGaloisAndArithmeticFundamentalGroups §IG.0.T4 for the constant-sheaf point-count
trace formula for all finite extensions, with the determinant expression supplied by
DeligneWeightsAndPurity §0.10. The
last is the only `ℓ`-adic geometric input, and it enters only the comparison of rigid and `ℓ`-adic Weil factors
([§RD.7.7](#rd-7-7) and [§RD.7.8](#rd-7-8)).

## Conventions

Unless a target says otherwise, `K` is a complete discretely valued field of characteristic 0 with
valuation ring `O_K`, uniformiser `π` and residue field `k` of characteristic `p`. Perfectness, algebraic
closure and finiteness of `k` are separate hypotheses, stated where used. The Laurent carriers also
make sense over a general complete nontrivially valued nonarchimedean field, and each theorem
states what it needs beyond that. In mixed characteristic (0,p), coefficient absolute values
restrict to the standard p-adic absolute value, `|p|=p⁻¹`; the separate additive degree valuation `w`
remains normalised by `w(π)=1`. All annular radii are positive. `A(r,1)` consists of Laurent series
converging at every radius `ρ` with `r < ρ < 1`, with decay at both ends; its topology is Fréchet,
the Robba ring `R_K` is the locally convex inductive limit over `r`, and multiplication is convergent
Cauchy convolution. The bounded and integral Robba rings differ from the `π`-adically complete Amice
ring, and on `O_E` the weak topology differs from the `π`-adic one. The coefficient rings are defined
before any Frobenius lift is chosen; extending a lift analytically changes the radius of the
annulus.

A connection is linear over the constant field and satisfies the Leibniz rule over the coefficient
ring. A Frobenius structure is an invertible horizontal linearisation `σ^*M → M` of a semilinear
map, where `σ_K` reduces to the `q`-power map, `q = p^a`; when `σ_K` is not onto, bijectivity of the
semilinear map itself is a separate statement. Integral Frobenius lattices used for unit-root
comparisons require an integral inverse, not only a stable lattice. Local degrees use `v_π = w`, with `v_π(π) = 1`:
`π^c` in rank one has slope `c` and the standard block `M_(c,d)` has slope `c/d`. Write `v_p(p) = 1`,
`e = v_π(p)` and `a = v_p(q)` for `q = p^a`. Cohomological slopes use `v_q = v_p/a`, so
`v_π = e · v_p = e · a · v_q` and `v_p = a · v_q`. Thus a uniformiser-normalised slope `s`
becomes `s/(e · a)` in the `q`-normalisation, while a p-normalised slope becomes `s/a`.
Differential breaks concern horizontal convergence and are unrelated to Frobenius slopes.

For radius variation write `η = e^(−r)`, order extrinsic subsidiary radii increasingly, and sum the
largest negative logarithms. A trivial `t`-differential line has extrinsic radius `η` and intrinsic
radius 1, hence extrinsic profile `r` and intrinsic profile 0. Coefficient derivations in several
variables commute and are of rational type. Bounded Teichmüller coefficients and their completion
are not identified with the Amice coefficients merely because both are written `E†` and `E`. In the
equal-characteristic Hartl–Pink convention `φ^r = π^(−d)`, so the arithmetic slope is `−d/r` while the
geometric degree is `d`. The global convergent slope filtration is increasing; the generic descent
over bounded rings uses the decreasing arithmetic convention stated at its target.

A frame is `X ⊂ Y ⊂ P` with `X` open in `Y` and `Y` closed in a formal scheme `P` smooth near `X`; properness
of `Y` is an extra hypothesis. The classical rigid tube uses the classical specialisation; for a
closed `T` the adic tube is the interior of its inverse image under the continuous specialisation.
Strict neighbourhoods and `j†` keep their boundary data. The weak fibration theorem gives an open
polydisc over a tube; the strong fibration theorem compares cofinal systems of neighbourhoods with
polydisc radii tending to 1, and does not give a product with one fixed open unit polydisc over
every boundary point. Coherent modules with connection are overconvergent coefficients only under
the Taylor overconvergence condition; integrability alone does not suffice, while an invertible
horizontal Frobenius forces it under the smooth weak-lift hypotheses of [§RD.3.31](#rd-3-31).

`H_rig, H_c,rig` and `H_Z,rig` denote ordinary, compactly supported and closed-support rigid cohomology.
Log proper support keeps the chosen proper model `X` and its open `U`, and applies the support functor
to tube sheaves before derived specialisation; its boundary realisation is log convergent. Base
change and pushforward with compact supports must preserve the supports, not only the underlying de
Rham complexes. The residue pairing keeps its one-form: for `∂ = d`/dT it uses dT, and for
`∂ = (1 + T)d`/dT it uses dT/`(1 + T)`. At a boundary point with coefficient field
`K_i`, the local residue is `K_i`-valued; the global contribution is
`Tr_{K_i/K} ∘ Res_i`. Localization retains the separate `K_i` components, and the
global residue pairing and trace use the sum of these `K`-valued contributions.

Over `𝔽_q`, the cohomological Frobenius `F` is the linear `q`-Frobenius when `σ_K = id`. For an object supplied with a
p-Frobenius `φ` over `W(𝔽_q)`, that operator is semilinear and `φ^a` is linear; its characteristic
polynomial is that of the iterate. A specified `q`-Frobenius need not admit such a root. The twist `K(n)` multiplies `F` by `q^(−n)` and lowers weights by `2n`. Numerical purity uses a
given embedding `ι : K^alg → ℂ`. A real weight normalisation is a constant Frobenius line after a
finite extension of coefficients, not an integer Tate twist by a real number. Weil factors are
`P_i(T) = det(1 − TF)`, as with Mathlib's `Matrix.charpolyRev`. A Weil number is algebraic and has the
required absolute value at every complex embedding; purity at one `ι` alone says less.

For the Dwork isocrystal choose `π^(p−1) = −p` and `∇e = πe dx`, with Frobenius multiplier
`exp(π(x^q − x))`; its trace function is the inverse of the additive character determined by `π`. For
Kummer isocrystals use `∇e = a·e dt/t` and multiplier `t^((q−1)a)`; the trace is the corresponding
character of the norm. `p` is odd where the sign identity needs it. Tate modules are covariant, and
geometric Frobenius on étale `H¹` is the transpose of arithmetic Frobenius on the Tate module. A row
Frobenius matrix records the image of each basis vector in its row, so its a-fold twisted product
is `F^(σ^(a−1)) ⋯ F^σ F`; the column convention reverses the order, which changes characteristic
polynomials for `a ≥ 3`.

## How to read the build

Layer RD.0 is analytic commutative algebra: coefficient rings, their topologies and Frobenius
lifts, and dagger algebras with controlled lifting and Frobenius homotopies. Layer RD.1 develops
differential modules and Frobenius modules separately over these rings, and Layer RD.2 combines
them into the slope filtration and local monodromy theorems, ending with the comparison of
differential and ramification breaks. Layer RD.3 globalises: frames, tubes and the coefficient
categories; it also contains the global slope results, which need its convergent category. Layer
RD.4 defines rigid cohomology with supports and its comparison maps, including the constant
rigid–crystalline comparison map needed by the trace in Layer RD.5. Layer RD.5 proves finiteness,
descent, duality, full faithfulness and semistable reduction, Layer RD.6 the trace formula and
p-adic Weil II, and Layer RD.7 the comparisons of Weil factors and their applications. The *Needs* clauses determine the construction order; the log support comparison RD.4.54 follows the compact-support amplitude theorem RD.5.78 that it uses. Each target states its hypotheses, gives a proof
sketch with source locators, lists what it *Needs* (earlier targets, library declarations and
sections of other roadmaps), and closes with **Checks**: computations, degenerate cases,
comparisons with library notions and non-examples that a wrong formalisation would fail.

- `CategoryTheory.RightRigidCategory`: Right rigid monoidal categories (duals), part of the Tannakian hypotheses. Used in RD.6.64.
- `CategoryTheory.Sheaf`: Sheaves on a site with values in a category; the overconvergent site is a site and its modules are sheaves on it. Used in RD.4.5, RD.5.68.
- `CategoryTheory.ShortComplex.SnakeInput`: The snake lemma, for the six-term sequence of generic pushforwards. Used in RD.5.50.
- `CochainComplex`: Cochain complexes (de Rham complexes). Used in RD.4.1.
- `Derivation`: Constant-linear derivation with Leibniz rule; a connection is linear over constants, not over its differential field. Used in RD.0.36, RD.1.1, RD.1.2, RD.1.3, RD.3.28.
- `DerivedCategory`: The derived category of an abelian category, assuming HasDerivedCategory; the homotopy localization and triangle machinery are imported, not new rigid-cohomology carriers. Used in RD.4.5, RD.4.10, RD.4.12, RD.4.39, RD.4.46.
- `Differential`: A commutative ring with a chosen derivation Derivation `ℤ R R`. Used in RD.1.1.
- `DiscreteConvolution.ringConvolution`: A total tsum convolution operation on coefficient functions, and addRingConvolution via `to_additive`. Summability hypotheses are required for associativity and analytic closure; this definition alone supplies no ring structure on arbitrary Laurent families or Robba germs. Used in RD.0.1.
- `ExteriorAlgebra.exteriorPower`: The `n`-th exterior power ⋀`[R]^n M` (used for `deg M = deg ∧^n M`). Used in RD.1.25.
- `FDRep`: Finite-dimensional representations of a monoid as a rigid monoidal category, the target `Rep_K(G)` for finite groups. Used in RD.6.64.
- `Field.absoluteGaloisGroup`: The absolute Galois group `Aut`(AlgebraicClosure `K/K`) with its profinite topology; restriction identifies it with `Gal(F^sep/F)`, the form used here. Used in RD.2.18, RD.2.24.
- `FiniteDimensional`: Finite-dimensional vector spaces (the finiteness conclusions and near-isomorphisms). Used in RD.5.23, RD.5.51.
- `HahnSeries`: Hahn (generalised power) series with well-founded support. Used in RD.5.2.
- `HenselianLocalRing`: Henselian local rings: simple roots of monic polynomials over the residue field lift. Used in RD.0.8, RD.0.26, RD.2.11, RD.2.18.
- `HenselianRing`: Henselian pairs `(R, I): I` in the Jacobson radical and simple roots modulo `I` lift. Used in RD.0.26.
- `HomologicalComplex.homology`: Homology of a complex: the cohomology of de Rham complexes. Used in RD.4.1, RD.5.53.
- `IsAlgClosed`: Algebraically closed fields. Used in RD.0.51, RD.1.32, RD.1.60.
- `IsAlgClosed.exists_pow_nat_eq`: In an algebraically closed field every element has an `n`-th root for `n > 0`. Used in RD.0.33.
- `IsAlgClosed.of_denseRange`: A complete nonarchimedean normed field of characteristic zero with a dense algebraically closed subfield is algebraically closed (CharZero hypothesis; proof via Krasner's lemma). Used in RD.0.33.
- `IsAlgClosed.of_exists_root`: A field in which every monic irreducible polynomial has a root is algebraically closed. Used in RD.0.33.
- `IsBezout`: The existing class saying every finitely generated ideal is principal. Used in RD.0.18, RD.0.24, RD.0.29, RD.0.30.
- `IsDiscreteValuationRing`: Discrete valuation rings: local PIDs that are not fields. Used in RD.0.8, RD.0.26.
- `IsGalois`: Galois field extensions (separable and normal). Used in RD.2.11, RD.2.18.
- `IsGalois.mem_range_algebraMap_iff_fixed`: For a finite Galois extension `E/F`, an element of `E` lies in `F` exactly when every automorphism in `Gal(E/F)` fixes it. Used in RD.7.5.
- `IsIntegrallyClosed.eq_map_mul_C_of_dvd`: Gauss's lemma: over an integrally closed domain `R` with fraction field `K`, a divisor in `K[X]` of a monic polynomial over `R` is, after normalising its leading coefficient, the image of a polynomial over `R`. Used in RD.7.4, RD.7.5.
- `IsNilpotent`: Nilpotent elements (the residue of a unipotent `∇`-module). Used in RD.2.16.
- `IsNoetherianRing`: Noetherian rings (dagger algebras, Lemma 7.3.4). Used in RD.5.51.
- `IsPrimitiveRoot`: Primitive roots of unity, for `ζ_π = θ(1)`. Used in RD.6.46.
- `IsPrincipalIdealRing`: Rings all of whose ideals are principal. Used in RD.0.14, RD.3.27.
- `LieModule.isNilpotent_derivedSeries_of_traceForm_eq_zero`: Cartan's criterion: if the trace form of a finite free representation `M` vanishes, then ⁅`L, L`⁆ acts nilpotently on `M` (characteristic zero domain). Used in RD.6.72.
- `LieModule.isNilpotent_iff_forall`: Engel's theorem: a Lie module is nilpotent iff every element acts nilpotently (`L` noetherian). Used in RD.6.72.
- `LieModule.traceForm`: The trace form `(x, y) ↦ Tr(ρ(x)ρ(y))` of a finite free representation. Used in RD.6.72.
- `LinearMap`: Bundled linear and semilinear maps, without an analytic convergence or connection structure. Used in RD.1.3.
- `LinearMap.IsPerfPair`: Perfect pairings (bijective in both arguments): the form of Poincaré duality. Used in RD.5.89.
- `LinearMap.index`: The `index dim ker f − dim coker f` of a linear map (a junk value unless kernel and cokernel are finite dimensional). Used in RD.5.23, RD.5.32.
- `LinearMap.index_comp`: Additivity of the index under composition of maps with finite-dimensional kernels and cokernels over a division ring. Used in RD.5.23, RD.5.32.
- `LinearMap.charpoly`: Characteristic polynomial of an endomorphism of a finite free module (Frobenius on cohomology). Used in RD.4.17, RD.6.2, RD.6.4.
- `LinearMap.ker`: The kernel submodule of a (semi)linear map; the light support-section illustration uses this existing carrier. Used in RD.4.42, RD.5.23.
- `LinearMap.range`: The image submodule of a linear map, used for the theta quotient. Used in RD.4.60.
- `LinearMap.trace`: The trace of an endomorphism of a finite free module, used on finite-dimensional cohomology. Used in RD.6.5, RD.6.15, RD.6.16.
- `Matrix.charpolyRev`: The reverse characteristic polynomial `det(1 − X·M)` of a square matrix; the convention of the Weil factors and of Tuitman's `χ(T)`. Used in RD.6.2, RD.7.18.
- `Matrix.det`: Determinant of a finite square matrix over a commutative ring. Used in RD.1.4, RD.1.25.
- `Matrix.reverse_charpoly`: The reverse of the characteristic polynomial equals charpolyRev. Used in RD.7.18.
- `Module.Basis`: A basis Module.Basis `ι R M`, indexed by an arbitrary type `ι` and represented by a linear equivalence `M ≃ₗ[R] (ι →₀ R)`; used here with `ι =` Fin `n`. Used in RD.0.47, RD.0.48, RD.1.3.
- `Module.Basis.equivFunL`: A finite basis gives a continuous linear equivalence with its coordinate space, over a complete nontrivially normed field and a Hausdorff topological vector space. Used in RD.0.17.
- `Module.Dual`: The algebraic dual `V →ₗ[K] K`. Supplies finite-dimensional coefficient duals only; continuous strong duals and their topology in [§RD.5.41](#rd-5-41) are separate targets, not this abbreviation. Used in RD.4.17, RD.5.41.
- `Module.FaithfullyFlat`: Faithfully flat modules. Used in RD.0.32.
- `Module.Flat.flat_iff_torsion_eq_bot_of_isBezout`: Over a Bézout domain a module is flat iff it is torsion-free. Used in RD.0.30; this criterion is consumed without a new flatness target.
- `Module.Free`: Free modules (existence of a basis). Used in RD.0.30, RD.3.27.
- `Module.Projective`: Projective modules. Used in RD.0.30, RD.3.27.
- `Nat.choose`: Binomial coefficients. Used in RD.6.36.
- `Padic`: The p-adic numbers `ℚ_[p]` with their norm (coefficient growth of the Liouville sequence). Used in RD.3.52.
- `PadicInt`: The p-adic integers `ℤ_[p]` as the elements of `ℚ_[p]` of norm at most 1 (exponents of Kummer isocrystals). Used in RD.3.51, RD.3.52.
- `PerfectClosure`. Used in RD.0.51.
- `PerfectField`: Perfect fields (every irreducible polynomial is separable). Algebraically closed fields are perfect by the instance IsAlgClosed.perfectField, which lives in Mathlib/FieldTheory/IsAlgClosed/Basic.lean. Used in RD.0.33.
- `Polynomial`: Polynomials (Lemma 5.2.7). Used in RD.5.17.
- `Polynomial.Splits`. Used in RD.1.60.
- `Polynomial.dvd_iff_isRoot`: `X−C(a)` divides a polynomial iff evaluation at a is zero, over a commutative ring. Used in RD.0.43.
- `Polynomial.evalRingHom`: Evaluation at a ring element is a ring homomorphism over a commutative semiring. Used in RD.0.43.
- `Polynomial.exists_aroots_norm_sub_lt_of_norm_coeff_sub_lt`: Continuity of roots: if monic `f, g` of equal degree have close coefficients and `g` splits in an extension, every root of `f` is close to a root of `g`; no separability or characteristic hypothesis. Used in RD.0.33.
- `Polynomial.exists_monic_and_natDegree_eq_and_norm_map_algebraMap_coeff_sub_lt`: For a dense subfield `K` of a normed field `L`, every monic polynomial over `L` is approximated coefficientwise by a monic polynomial over `K` of the same degree. Used in RD.0.33.
- `Polynomial.reverse`: Reversed polynomials, for `det(1 − tF)` as the reverse of the characteristic polynomial. Used in RD.6.89.
- `Polynomial.roots`: Multiset of roots of a polynomial with multiplicities. Used in RD.6.28.
- `PowerSeries`: Formal power series `R[[X]]`. Used in RD.6.4.
- `PowerSeries.derivative`: The formal derivative of power series as a derivation `R⟦X⟧ → R⟦X⟧`. Used in RD.0.36.
- `PowerSeries.exp`: The exponential power series over a `Q`-algebra, for `exp(π(x^σ − x))` and zeta functions. Used in RD.6.22, RD.6.42, RD.6.46.
- `PowerSeries.ext`: Two formal power series with the same coefficients are equal; the identities of [§RD.7.4](#rd-7-4) are coefficientwise. Used in RD.7.4.
- `PowerSeries.mk`: Power series from coefficient sequences, for zeta functions and Hankel determinants. Used in RD.6.22, RD.6.24.
- `RatFunc`: Rational functions over a field, the target of rationality statements. Used in RD.6.24.
- `Representation`: Linear representations of a monoid on a module: a monoid hom to the endomorphisms. Used in RD.2.24, RD.2.35.
- `SkewPolynomial`: Polynomial carrier with multiplication twisted by a MulSemiringAction: `X·a = φ(a)·X`. Supplies a multiplicative Frobenius-twist analogue after the action instance is provided; it does not supply differential Ore multiplication `X·a = a·X + δ(a)`. Used in RD.1.2, RD.1.21.
- `Submodule.FG`: Finitely generated submodules (Lemma 7.3.4, finiteness of local cohomology). Used in RD.5.51.
- `Submodule.mkQ`: The quotient projection `M→M/S` with its existing module structure. Used in RD.4.60, RD.5.23.
- `TensorProduct`: Tensor products of modules, for the Künneth maps of complexes of K-vector spaces. Used in RD.3.28, RD.4.17, RD.5.92, RD.5.93.
- `UniformSpace.Completion`: The Hausdorff completion of a uniform space. Used in RD.0.33.
- `WithSeminorms`: A topology induced by an indexed family of seminorms over a normed field; no real or complex scalar assumption. Used in RD.0.2, RD.5.40.
- `WithSeminorms.continuous_of_isBounded`: Continuity of an isometrically semilinear map bounded by finite families of source seminorms. Used in RD.0.2.
- `WittVector`: p-typical Witt vectors `W(R)` with coefficients x.coeff `n`. Used in RD.0.6, RD.0.54.
- `WittVector.Isocrystal`: Isocrystals over a perfect field `k`: vector spaces over `K(p,k) = FractionRing (WittVector p k)` with a Frobenius-semilinear automorphism; the fibres of F-isocrystals at perfect points. Used in RD.1.21, RD.3.34, RD.3.36, RD.3.47, RD.3.48, RD.6.2.
- `WittVector.StandardOneDimIsocrystal`: The one-dimensional isocrystal of slope `m ∈ ℤ`, with Frobenius `x ↦ p^m φ(x)`. Used in RD.3.34.
- `WittVector.ext`: Equality of all Witt coordinates implies equality of Witt vectors. Used in RD.0.52.
- `WittVector.frobenius`: The p-typical Witt Frobenius ring endomorphism for any commutative coefficient ring; in characteristic `p` its coefficients are p-th powers. Used in RD.0.5, RD.0.6, RD.6.1.
- `WittVector.isocrystal_classification`: Over an algebraically closed `k` every one-dimensional isocrystal is isomorphic to StandardOneDimIsocrystal `p k m` for some `m ∈ ℤ`. Used in RD.1.23, RD.1.32, RD.3.47.
- `WittVector.map`: Functorial ring homomorphism on Witt vectors induced by a coefficient ring homomorphism. Used in RD.0.52.
- `WittVector.map_coeff`: WittVector.map acts on every Witt coordinate by the input ring homomorphism. Used in RD.0.52.
- `WittVector.teichmuller`: The Teichmüller lift `R →* W(R)` (multiplicative, 0-th coefficient `r`, others 0). Used in RD.0.6.
- `padicValNat_factorial`: Legendre: `v_p(n!) = Σ_{1 ≤ i < b} ⌊n/p^i⌋` for `b > log_p n`. Used in RD.6.35.
- `padicValRat`: p-adic valuation on `ℚ` (denominator bound of Lemma 5.2.7). Used in RD.5.17, RD.6.58.
- `spectralNorm.normedField`: An algebraic extension `L` of a complete nonarchimedean normed field `K` is a normed field under the spectral norm. Used in RD.0.33.
- `spectralNorm_extends`: The spectral norm restricts to the given norm on `K`. Used in RD.0.33.
- `sub_one_mul_padicValNat_factorial`: Legendre: `(p − 1)·v_p(n!) = n −` (sum of base-`p` digits of `n`). Used in RD.6.30, RD.6.35.

- `AddChar.compAddMonoidHom`: pullback of a character through the additive field trace; RD.6.46 uses this with `AddChar.zmodChar`, without a second character carrier.
- `Topology.IsStrictMap`, `LinearMap.isStrictMap_iff_isHomeomorph_quotKerEquivRange` and `LinearMap.isStrictMap_iff_isOpenQuotientMap_rangeRestrict`: Bourbaki strictness and its quotient/range and open-range descriptions. Used in RD.5.41–RD.5.44.
- `LinearMap.mem_ker`, `LinearMap.ker_zero` and `LinearMap.ker_id`: section-level support kernels and their empty/full-complement cases. Used in RD.4.42.
- `CategoryTheory.EssentiallySmall`: a small skeleton in the specified universe; used in RD.6.64 so that the representing Hopf algebra belongs to that universe.
- `LinearMap.isStrictMap_prodMap_iff`: strictness of a finite product is componentwise; used with closedness of product ranges in RD.5.41.
- `Submodule.liftQ` and `Submodule.Quotient.subsingleton_iff`: the universal map out of a range quotient, and its vanishing when the range is the full module. Used for the module-level theta presentation in RD.4.60.

### From Tau Ceti (pinned at `a91d3aafa8cd3e6bc33dfde0d7677ed0f1625039`)

- `TauCeti.LocalFieldsRamification.herbrand`, `TauCeti.LocalFieldsRamification.inverseHerbrand` and `TauCeti.LocalFieldsRamification.upperRamificationGroup`: the Herbrand order isomorphism on `[-1, ∞)`, its inverse and upper ramification groups for finite Galois extensions of nonarchimedean local fields. Their finite-residue-field domain is used in RD.2.44–RD.2.47 and RD.6.51; LocalFieldsRamification Layers 3–4 supply the general perfect-residue-field ramification package, agreeing with these declarations on the common domain.
- `LinearMap.trace_eq_add_of_exact`: For an endomorphism of a short exact sequence `0 → N → M → Q → 0` of vector spaces with `M` finite-dimensional, trace `f =` trace `f_N +` trace `f_Q`. Used in RD.6.20.
- `TauCeti.FGComoduleCat`: Finitely generated right comodules over a coalgebra, as a full subcategory of all comodules (finite-dimensional comodules over a field); the category `Rep_K(G)` of the recognition theorem. Used in RD.6.64.
- `TauCeti.FGComoduleCat.instRigidCategory`: Finite-dimensional comodules over a commutative Hopf algebra over a field form a rigid monoidal category. Used in RD.6.64.
- `TauCeti.FGComoduleCat.instSymmetricCategory`: The symmetric monoidal structure (tensor-product swap) on finite comodules over a commutative bialgebra. Used in RD.6.64.
- `TauCeti.GaloisDescent.liftBaseChange_injective_of_invariant`: Over a finite Galois `L/k`, an injective `k`-linear map into invariant vectors stays injective after scalar extension to `L` (Hilbert-Noether descent, injectivity half). Used in RD.2.24, RD.2.35.
- `TauCeti.GaloisDescent.span_invariants_eq_top`: For a field `L` with finite automorphism group over `k`, the invariant vectors of a semilinear representation span it over `L` (Hilbert-Noether descent, surjectivity half). Used in RD.2.24, RD.2.35.
- `TauCeti.Tannaka.fgPointTensorIsoEquiv`: For a commutative Hopf algebra `H` over a field `k` and a commutative `k`-algebra `A`, A-valued points of `H` are equivalent (as groups) to tensor automorphisms of scalar extension to A on finite-dimensional `H`-comodules. Used in RD.2.51.
- `TauCeti.Tannaka.pointsFunctorIsoTensorAutFunctor`: Tannakian reconstruction for a commutative Hopf algebra `H` over a field: the functor of points of `H` is isomorphic, naturally in the commutative algebra `A`, to the group functor of tensor automorphisms of scalar extension to A on finite `H`-comodules (pointwise form TauCeti.Tannaka.fgPointTensorIsoEquiv). Used in RD.2.51, RD.6.64.
- `TauCeti.finiteDimensional_quotient_repartitionSpace`: For an algebraic function field `F/k` with exact constants and a divisor `D, A_F/(A_F(D) + F)` is finite dimensional over `k` (Stichtenoth 1.5.4). Used in RD.5.25.
- `TauCeti.finiteDimensional_riemannRochSpace`: Riemann–Roch spaces `L(D)` of a function field are finite dimensional over `k` (Stichtenoth 1.4.9). Used in RD.5.25.
- `TauCeti.finrank_quotient_repartitionSpace_zero`: `g = dim_k A_F/(A_F(0) + F)` (Stichtenoth 1.5.5): the cokernel of principal parts has dimension the genus. Used in RD.5.25.
- `TauCeti.finrank_weilDifferentialFiltration_zero`: The regular Weil differentials form a `k`-space of dimension the genus (Stichtenoth 1.5.12). Used in RD.5.25.
- `TauCeti.genus`: The genus of an algebraic function field. Used in RD.5.25, RD.6.53.
- `WeierstrassCurve.frobeniusTrace`: For a Weierstrass model over a finite field with `q` elements, the integer `q + 1 − #W(F)` (projective count); on an elliptic model it is the classical trace `a_q (frobeniusTrace_eq_card_point)`. Used in RD.7.11, RD.7.17.

### From TauCetiRoadmap

- AdicSpaces: adic spectra, rational subsets and the analytic vocabulary on which AdicSpacesPartII builds; used throughout Layers RD.3–RD.5 through AdicSpacesPartII.
- LocalFieldsRamification, Layers 3–4: finite and absolute lower/upper ramification, Herbrand functions, subgroup and quotient compatibility, upper numbering on open subgroups, invariance under completed maximal unramified base change and the full Hasse–Arf theorem over complete discretely valued fields with any perfect residue field. The finite lower groups use `Ideal.ramificationGroup` and the real-indexed `TauCeti.IsLocalRing.ramificationGroupReal`; on finite residue fields this package agrees with the pinned Tau Ceti declarations listed above. ArithmeticGaloisRepresentations Layer 3 supplies representation breaks and conductors on this filtration, and [§RD.2.45](#rd-2-45) extends their coefficient domain.
- AlgebraicCurves, Layer 9: Kähler differentials of a function field are identified with Weil differentials compatibly with residues; regular differentials have dimension `g` and principal parts at the missing points of an affine curve have one-dimensional cokernel (residue theorem). Used in the index computation for affine curves ([§RD.5.25](#rd-5-25)).
- EllipticCurves, Layer 3: an elliptic curve over `𝔽_q` is supersingular if and only if `p` divides its Frobenius trace. Used in [§RD.7.11](#rd-7-11).
- JacobianChallenge, Layer `F`: the Jacobian of a smooth proper geometrically connected curve with a rational point after a finite extension, the Abel–Jacobi map and its universal property for maps to abelian varieties. Used in [§RD.6.62](#rd-6-62).
- FormalLaurentPuiseux §L3: formal Laurent residues, their coordinate formula and coefficient duality; the Robba LF duality of RD.5.45 has two-sided analytic tails and a different topology.
- CompactOperators §§1.2–1.5 and §3.2: principal-minor Fredholm coefficients, cyclicity, (Pr)-module determinants and nonzero generalized eigenspaces. Used in RD.6.5, RD.6.7 and RD.6.16–RD.6.17.
- PadicFunctionalAnalysis §§1.2, 1.3, 2.2: Banach-source mapping theorems, orthogonal families and topological bases; RD.5.40 extends the Banach-source uniform-boundedness theorem to barrelled locally convex spaces, and RD.0.47 asks for the algebraic-basis comparison with finite coordinate support, without assuming a complete ambient module.
- ReductiveGroups, Layers 1–3: affine algebraic groups, their Lie algebras and the adjoint representation, components and quotients. Used in [§RD.6.71](#rd-6-71).
- EtaleCohomologyFoundations §§`F`.0.2, `F`.0.A2 (étale fundamental groups, fibre-functor equivalence and the arithmetic fundamental-group sequence) and InverseGaloisAndArithmeticFundamentalGroups §IG.0.T4 (for `X` separated of finite type over `𝔽_q` and `ℓ ≠ p`, the identity `#X(𝔽_{q^r}) = Σ_i (−1)^i Tr(Frob_q^r | Hⁱ_c(X_𝔽̄_q, ℚ_ℓ))` for every `r ≥ 1`); DeligneWeightsAndPurity §0.10 supplies the determinant expression of the zeta function. Used in [§RD.3.43a](#rd-3-43a) and [§RD.3.48](#rd-3-48) and in the `ℓ`-adic comparisons [§RD.7.7](#rd-7-7) and [§RD.7.8](#rd-7-8).

## Layer RD.0: Coefficient rings and analytic foundations

This layer constructs the coefficient rings and proves their analytic properties. It defines the
Laurent, Robba, bounded, integral and Amice coefficient rings with their Fréchet, inductive-limit,
valuation and weak topologies before any Frobenius lift is chosen; then the Frobenius lift on the
integral Amice ring by weak substitution, its extension to the bounded and full Robba rings with the
accompanying change of radius, and the Taylor formula for a change of lift. Kedlaya's analytic rings
`Γ_I, Γ_an,r` and `Γ_an,con`, the identification of the Robba ring among them, and the extended Robba ring
over a completed algebraic closure follow, with semiunit presentations, matrix factorisation, the
Bézout property, closed ideals and analytic divisors (after Lazard), modules over Bézout domains and
valuation p-bases. The dagger half proves existence of Frobenius lifts on Monsky–Washnitzer algebras
and their uniqueness up to homotopy, through Arabia's controlled lifting and an explicit rational
chain homotopy. The layer ends with the coefficient rings of Fargues–Fontaine in both coefficient
characteristics.

<a id="rd-0-1"></a>

### RD.0.1 Laurent, Robba and Amice coefficient carriers

**Definition.** For a complete nontrivially nonarchimedean normed field `K`, define `A(r,1)`, for `0 < r < 1`, by the Laurent coefficient families `(a_n)` with `|a_n|ρ^n` tending to zero as `|n|` tends to infinity for every `r < ρ < 1`; multiply by convergent Cauchy convolution. Define `R_K` as their directed union, with each `A(r,1)` carrying its radius-indexed Fréchet topology and `R_K` its locally convex inductive-limit topology. Define `R^bd` by bounded coefficients and `R^int` by integral coefficients. For the Amice ring `E` require bounded coefficients and `a_n → 0` as `n → −∞; O_E` is its integral part. These carrier definitions also make sense in equal characteristic; the differential and Frobenius statements below impose their own characteristic hypotheses. For discretely valued `K, O_E` is the integral part of `E, R^bd = R^int[1/π]` and `E = O_E[1/π]`. These are coefficient carriers before a Frobenius lift is chosen; their chart, inductive-limit, valuation and weak topologies are specified separately.

*Hypotheses.*

- `K` is complete and nontrivially nonarchimedean. The integral and valuation-field assertions additionally require `K` discretely valued with uniformiser `π`.
- Every annulus radius is positive; convergence is required at every interior radius, at both Laurent tails.

The API:

- `annulusCoeffs`: The K-submodule of coefficient families converging at every positive radius `r < ρ < 1`, for `0 < r < 1`.
- `robbaCoeffs`: The directed union of annulusCoeffs over `0 < r < 1`.
- `RobbaRing`: The subtype of robbaCoeffs with convergent Cauchy multiplication and its K-algebra structure.
- `amiceCoeffs`: Bounded coefficient families tending to zero at the negative end.
- `AmiceRing`: The coefficient subtype of amiceCoeffs with its valuation-field structure when `K` is discretely valued.
- `gaussNorm`: At `ρ > 0` where the series converges, `sup_n |a_n|ρ^n`. Outside this domain the total real-valued prototype has no norm interpretation.
- `RobbaRing.bounded`: The bounded-coefficient subring of `R_K`.
- `RobbaRing.integral`: The subring of `R_K` with every coefficient of norm at most one.
- `RobbaRing.coe_mul`: Coefficients of multiplication equal convergent discrete convolution, rather than pointwise multiplication.

*Proof sketch.* Construct the Laurent subalgebras by radius-wise summability of convolution. Positive radii are mandatory. Define restriction, Gauss norms only at radii of convergence, the directed union and its final locally convex topology. This is the coefficient construction of Kedlaya, overview Definition 3.5.1, before the Cohen/Witt comparison. The precise topologies are [§RD.0.2](#rd-0-2) and the field extensions [§RD.0.17](#rd-0-17); both are stated on these underlying coefficient carriers. Define bounded and integral coefficient subrings and the complete bounded Amice carrier. Multiplication is convergent Cauchy convolution, not pointwise multiplication; the negative-tail condition makes reduction an element of `k((t))`. (Kedlaya, *Local monodromy of p-adic differential equations: an overview*, Definition 3.5.1, p. 15; Kedlaya, *A p-adic local monodromy theorem*, §2.3, pp. 12–14.)

*Needs:* Mathlib `DiscreteConvolution.ringConvolution`.

**Checks.**

- `robba_coordinate_inverse`: The Laurent monomials `t` and `t^−1` multiply to 1.
- `robba_constants_coefficients`: The constant series `C(c)` has coefficient `c` at 0 and zero at all nonzero indices.
- `robba_negative_tail_nonexample`: The coefficient family equal to 1 at every negative index and 0 elsewhere belongs neither to `R_K` nor to `E`.
- In the special case of a perfect residue field `k, K=W(k)[1/p], q=p` and the standard lift `σ(t)=t^p`, this target agrees with FiniteFlatGroupsAndIntegralPadicHodgeTheory §§R07.4.7–R07.4.8: the same coefficient carriers, degree convention, standard blocks and increasing slope filtration. This roadmap adds the general coefficients and Frobenius lifts.

<a id="rd-0-2"></a>

### RD.0.2 Laurent Fréchet charts and the Robba inductive limit

**Construction.** On the Laurent carrier define `A_K(I)` for a nonempty interval `I` of positive multiplicative radii by convergence at every radius in `I`. At radius `ρ` use `|f|_ρ = sup_n |a_n|ρ^n`. On each compact window `J=[α,β]` inside `I` use `p_J=max(|·|_α,|·|_β)`. `A_K(I)` carries the separated complete topology generated by these seminorms and is their compatible projective limit; a compact `I` gives its Banach norm `p_I`. For a disc containing the centre use only `n≥0` and include evaluation at zero. Identify this positive-power chart coefficientwise with RestrictedPowerSeries §§1.1–1.2 for a closed disc and §7.1 for an open disc: these are `K`-algebra isomorphisms preserving each Gauss seminorm, hence homeomorphisms. They intertwine restrictions, polynomial inclusions and evaluation, including at zero; the disc completeness and projective-limit descriptions are transported from that supplier. `R_K` is the union of `A_K((r,1))`, with the nonarchimedean locally convex inductive-limit topology of LocallyAnalyticDistributions Layer 0 (the finest locally convex topology making all chart inclusions continuous); each `A_K(I)` is the L0 projective limit of its compact-window Banach charts. A cofinal sequence `r_j` increasing to 1 gives the same locally convex inductive limit (LF) topology. No strictness, bounded-set factorisation or completeness of this inductive limit is assumed.

*Hypotheses.*

- `K` is complete, nontrivially nonarchimedean, of either characteristic.
- Compact positive-radius annuli may have arbitrary real endpoints; no assumption that the value group is discrete.
- Locally convex is meant in the nonarchimedean sense of LocallyAnalyticDistributions §0.0 (ultrametric seminorms and open lattices), which rests on the pinned WithSeminorms API rather than on Mathlib’s real convexity predicates. The Gauss seminorms `|·|_ρ` and `p_J` are ultrametric.

The API:

- `LaurentChart.withSeminorms`: The topology is WithSeminorms for the compact-window Gauss family on the carrier.
- `LaurentChart.isNALocallyConvex`: Each `A_K(I)`, and `R_K`, is a Hausdorff nonarchimedean locally convex K-space in the sense of LocallyAnalyticDistributions Layer 0 (IsNALocallyConvex): `A_K(I)` is the L0 projective limit of its compact-window Banach charts and `R_K` the L0 inductive limit of the charts `A_K((r,1))`.
- `LaurentChart.restrict`: For `J⊆I`, restriction `A_K(I)→A_K(J)` is an injective continuous K-algebra map and composes strictly on coefficients.
- `LaurentChart.complete`: `A_K(I)` is complete and Hausdorff; the compact endpoint maximum is its Banach norm.
- `RobbaRing.continuous_linear_iff`: A K-linear map from `R_K` to a nonarchimedean locally convex K-space is continuous iff its restriction to every `A_K((r,1))` is continuous; this is the L0 continuity criterion for inductive limits `(naInductiveLimit_continuous_iff)` applied to the chart system.
- `RobbaRing.cofinal_charts`: Every cofinal countable increasing family `r_j→1` yields the same union and the same final seminorm topology.
- `LaurentChart.mul_bound`: `p_J`(fg)`≤p_J(f)p_J(g)`; constants have Gauss norm `|c|` and `|t^n|_ρ=ρ^n`.

*Proof sketch.*

1. Use the coefficient carrier and convolution. Ultrametric summability gives the submultiplicative Gauss bounds; truncation by finite Laurent polynomials converges on every compact positive-radius window.
2. Construct the compact completion as weighted two-sided null sequences. Compatible coefficient limits on a countable compact exhaustion give completeness and metrisability of `A_K(I)`; the topology does not depend on the exhaustion.
3. For discs extend a supplied coefficient family by zero at negative indices and restrict back to `ℕ`. These inverse maps preserve convolution, all Gauss seminorms and evaluation, giving the identifications with RestrictedPowerSeries. Give the existing Robba union the locally convex inductive-limit topology of LocallyAnalyticDistributions §0.0 `(i)`: a lattice is open exactly when its preimage in every chart is open, and a linear map out of `R_K` is continuous exactly when its restrictions to all charts are. Each chart is the projective limit of part (ii) over its compact windows. Chart restriction is injective and continuous; multiplication is continuous on every fixed chart and separately continuous on the union.

*Sources.* Lazard, *Les zéros des fonctions analytiques d’une variable sur un corps valué complet*, §2, (2.1)–(2.6) and Proposition 1, pp.50–51; Kedlaya, *Slope filtrations revisited*, Definition 2.4.2 and Remark 2.4.3, p. 14; Example 2.4.9, p. 15; Colmez–Fargues–Fontaine, *Préface to Courbes et fibrés vectoriels en théorie de Hodge p-adique*, Préface §2.5.1, p.24.

*Needs:* RestrictedPowerSeries §§1.1–1.2 *Closed-disc coefficient algebras* and §7.1 *Series on an open disc*; [§RD.0.1](#rd-0-1) *Laurent, Robba and Amice coefficient carriers*; Mathlib `WithSeminorms`; Mathlib `WithSeminorms.continuous_of_isBounded`; LocallyAnalyticDistributions §0.0 *Locally convex spaces and separation*; LocallyAnalyticDistributions §0.0 *Locally convex limits*.

**Checks.**

- `chart_monomial_norm`: On `[α,β], p_J(t)=β` and `p_J(t⁻¹)=α⁻¹`; one endpoint cannot replace the maximum.
- `chart_positive_tail`: `Σ_{n≥0}t^n` converges on the open unit disc and on every compact subdisc, but not on the closed unit disc.
- `chart_equal_characteristic`: For `K=𝔽_p((z))`, the same annular coefficient conditions and Gauss norms apply; no Witt-vector or characteristic-zero hypothesis enters.
- `disc_centre`: A chart containing `t=0` contains constants and `t` but excludes `t⁻¹`; completing Laurent polynomials without excluding negative powers gives the wrong disc.
- Laurent-polynomial density is a chart-topology assertion, not `π`-adic density in `O_E`.
- Under the open-disc identification `Σ t^n` has Gauss seminorm `1` at each `0<r<1`, but its coefficients do not tend to zero at radius 1, so it is absent from the closed unit-disc algebra. Both carriers give value 1 at zero.

<a id="rd-0-3"></a>

### RD.0.3 The weak topology on the integral Amice ring

**Construction.** For `K` a complete discretely valued field with integers `O` and uniformiser `π`, give `O_E` the inverse-limit topology of `O_E/π^m≅(O/π^m)((t))`, where the latter has the additive `t`-adic topology: a series is small when every coefficient below a specified index is zero. Thus a fundamental neighbourhood of zero is `U(m,N)=`{`f: a_i∈π^m O` for all `i<N`}. Equivalently `f_j→0` iff for each `m` its reduction eventually has `t`-order tending to `+∞`. This topology is complete, Hausdorff and a ring topology, and is coarser than the `π`-adic topology. Finite Laurent polynomials are dense for it. The inverse-limit reductions are ring isomorphisms, not just bijections of coefficient sets.

*Hypotheses.*

- `K` may have either characteristic; `O` is a complete DVR.
- The coefficients of every `O_E` series are integral and tend `π`-adically to zero towards `−∞`.
- For each `m` a reduction has only finitely many negative terms, but may have infinitely many positive terms.

The API:

- `AmiceRing.integral_reduce`: For every `m≥1, O_E/π^m≅(O/π^m)((t))`, compatibly with coefficients, multiplication and transition maps.
- `AmiceRing.weak_nhds_zero`: The sets `U(m,N), m≥1` and `N∈Z`, form a neighbourhood basis at zero.
- `AmiceRing.weak_complete`: `O_E` is complete and separated for the inverse-limit `t`-adic uniformity.
- `AmiceRing.laurentPolynomial_weak_dense`: Finite Laurent polynomials over `O` are weak-dense in `O_E`.
- `AmiceRing.integralRobba_reduce`: `R^int/πR^int≅k((t))`; surjectivity is obtained by bounded lifts with finitely many negative indices, and the kernel is `πR^int`.

*Proof sketch.*

1. Reduction of convolution is formal Laurent multiplication because only finitely many summands survive in each coefficient modulo `π^m`.
2. Choose compatible coefficient lifts in `O` to identify `O_E` with the inverse limit of these Laurent series rings. This proves completeness and Hausdorffness of the levelwise topology.
3. The `t`-adic multiplication estimates on each quotient give the ring topology. Truncate both tails modulo `π^m` to prove weak density. Every `U(m,N)` contains `π^mO_E`, so the identity from the `π`-adic topology to the weak topology is continuous.

*Sources.* Kedlaya, *Slope filtrations revisited*, Definition 2.2.7, p. 8; Convention 2.3.1 and Definition 2.3.2, pp. 11–12.

*Needs:* [§RD.0.1](#rd-0-1) *Laurent, Robba and Amice coefficient carriers*; [§RD.0.2](#rd-0-2) *Laurent Fréchet charts and the Robba inductive limit*.

**Checks.**

- `weak_shift`: `t^n→0` weakly as `n→∞`, but `t^n` never lies in `πO_E`, so it does not tend to zero `π`-adically.
- `weak_geometric_tail`: `Σ_{i=0}^N t^i` converges weakly to `(1−t)⁻¹` in `O_E`; the same sequence is not `π`-adic Cauchy.
- `weak_negative_tail`: The family `Σ_{i<0}t^i` is not in `O_E`; reduction must be a Laurent series with a finite negative tail.
- `weak_nilpotent_coefficients`: For `m=2`, reduction is over `O/π²`, not merely over `k; πt^N` is nonzero there and still tends to zero `t`-adically.
<a id="rd-0-4"></a>

### RD.0.4 Weak convergence of semilinear Laurent substitution

**Theorem.** Let `σ_K:K→K` be an isometric ring endomorphism preserving `O` and inducing `q`-power Frobenius on `k, q=p^a` with `a≥1`. For `u∈R^int` with `u≡t^q` mod `π`, the series `Σ_i σ_K(a_i)u^i` converges in the weak topology for every `f=Σ_i a_i t^i∈O_E` and defines the unique weak-continuous `σ_K`-semilinear ring endomorphism with `t↦u`. Modulo `π` its action on `k((t))` is exactly the `q`-power map. It is `π`-adically continuous as well, but weak continuity is essential to its classification.

*Hypotheses.*

- Mixed characteristic for the Frobenius object; the weak-convergence lemma itself also applies in equal characteristic when the stated coefficient lift exists.
- `u` is overconvergent, not an arbitrary unit of `O_E`, when extending to analytic charts.

*Proof sketch.*

1. Modulo `π^m` write `u=t^q(1+h)` with `h∈π(O/π^m)((t))`. The inverse of `1+h` is the finite nilpotent geometric sum. Positive powers `u^i` have `t`-order at least qi`−C_m`, since only powers `h^j` with `j<m` survive; this estimate is uniform in `i`.
2. For the positive tail use that estimate, including `σ_K` on coefficients; for the negative tail `a_i` vanish modulo `π^m` once `i` is sufficiently negative. Thus both tails converge in every quotient.
3. Use finite polynomial substitution and continuity to obtain additivity, multiplicativity and uniqueness on the weak completion. For reduction, raising a Laurent series to `q` in characteristic `p` applies `q`-power to coefficients and multiplies every exponent by `q`.

*Sources.* Kedlaya, *Slope filtrations revisited*, Convention 2.3.1, p. 11, and Definitions 2.2.3 and 2.2.7, p. 8.

*Needs:* [§RD.0.3](#rd-0-3) *The weak topology on the integral Amice ring*; [§RD.0.1](#rd-0-1) *Laurent, Robba and Amice coefficient carriers*.

**Checks.**

- `σ(t⁻¹)=u⁻¹`.
- For `u=t^q` the formula sends `a_i t^i` to `σ_K(a_i)t^{qi}`.
- For `K=ℚ_p` and `u=(1+t)^p−1` the reduction is `t^p`, although `u` is not equal to `t^p`.

<a id="rd-0-5"></a>

### RD.0.5 Weakly continuous Frobenius lifts on the integral Amice ring

**Definition.** Use the coefficient carriers [§RD.0.1](#rd-0-1). Fix `K` complete discretely valued of characteristic 0 with ring of integers `O_K`, uniformiser `π`, residue field `k` of characteristic `p`, and a Frobenius lift `σ_K` on `K` (a continuous ring endomorphism with `σ_K(O_K) ⊆ O_K` reducing to `x ↦ x^q` on `k, q = p^a`). Let `O_E` be the ring of Laurent series `Σ_{i∈Z} a_i t^i` with `a_i ∈ O_K` and `a_i → 0` as `i → −∞` (the integral Amice ring; `E = O_E[1/π]`), let `R^int ⊆ O_E` be the series converging on some annulus `r < |t| < 1` (all coefficients integral), `R^bd = R^int[1/π]`, and `R` the Robba ring (constructed here from convergent coefficient families, before choosing a Frobenius lift). A Frobenius lift is a ring endomorphism `σ` of `O_E` that is `σ_K`-semilinear on `O_K`, continuous for the weak (levelwise) topology, and satisfies `σ(t) ∈ R^int` and `σ(t) − t^q ∈ π·R^int`. Such `σ` is determined by `u = σ(t)` through `σ(Σ a_i t^i) = Σ σ_K(a_i) u^i`; conversely every `u ∈ R^int` with `u ≡ t^q` mod `π` defines one. Extension to bounded and full Robba rings, with its radius change, is the theorem [§RD.0.46](#rd-0-46); it is not a condition in this definition.

*Hypotheses.*

- `K` is discretely valued; `π` is a uniformiser; `q = p^a` and `σ_K` induces the `q`-power map on `k`. When `k` is perfect and `K = W(k)[1/p], σ_K` may be taken to be (a power of) the Witt vector Frobenius.
- The condition `σ(t) ∈ R^int` is Kedlaya's overconvergence condition `lim inf_{i→−∞} w(a_i)/(−i) > 0` on the coefficients of `σ(t)` (slope filtrations revisited, Convention 2.3.1).
- A Frobenius lift need not be a power of a p-power Frobenius lift (slope filtrations revisited, Remark 2.2.5); the older monodromy paper requires a composition power of a lift of the p-power map.
- No ring of functions on a fixed annulus `r < |t| < 1` carries a Frobenius lift: `σ` moves the inner radius from `r` to `r^{1/q}`.

The API:

- `RobbaRing.FrobeniusLift`: A Frobenius lift: `σ_K` on `K` together with `u = σ(t) ∈ R^int` with `u − t^q ∈ π·R^int`; the ring endomorphism of `O_E` it induces.
- `RobbaRing.FrobeniusLift.ofImage`: For `u ∈ R^int` with `u ≡ t^q` mod `π` there is a unique Frobenius lift with `σ(t) = u`.
- `RobbaRing.FrobeniusLift.ext`: Two Frobenius lifts with the same `σ_K` and the same image of `t` are equal.
- `RobbaRing.FrobeniusLift.standard`: The standard lift `σ(t) = t^q, σ(Σ a_i t^i) = Σ σ_K(a_i) t^{qi}`.
- `RobbaRing.FrobeniusLift.reduction`: Modulo `π`, the weakly continuous lift on `O_E` induces `q`-power Frobenius on `O_E/πO_E = k((t))`. Preservation and reduction of `R^int` are consequences of [§RD.0.46](#rd-0-46).

*Proof sketch.* Existence and uniqueness from `u: O_E` is the `π`-adic completion of `O_K[[t]][t^{-1}]`; Laurent polynomials are dense for the weak levelwise topology, which is different from the `π`-adic topology (monodromy paper, Section 2.3), so a levelwise-continuous `σ` is determined by `σ(t)` and `σ_K; u` is a unit of `O_E` because its reduction `t^q` is a unit of `k((t))`, so `Σ σ_K(a_i) u^i` converges levelwise. Use [§RD.0.3](#rd-0-3) and [§RD.0.4](#rd-0-4) for the existence, uniqueness and reduction assertions. The extension theorem uses this lift after constructing the analytic comparison, and is not a prerequisite of the lift definition. (Kedlaya, *Slope filtrations revisited*, Definition 2.2.3 and Remark 2.2.5, p. 8, and Convention 2.3.1, pp. 11-12; Kedlaya, *A p-adic local monodromy theorem*, Section 1.1, p. 3, and Section 2.3, p. 12.)

*Needs:* [§RD.0.1](#rd-0-1) *Laurent, Robba and Amice coefficient carriers*; [§RD.0.3](#rd-0-3) *The weak topology on the integral Amice ring*; [§RD.0.4](#rd-0-4) *Weak convergence of semilinear Laurent substitution*; Mathlib `WittVector.frobenius`.

**Checks.**

- `frobeniusLift_standard_apply`: For the standard lift and `f = Σ a_i t^i` in `O_E: σ(f) = Σ σ_K(a_i) t^{qi}`; in particular `σ(t^{-1}) = t^{-q}`.
- `frobeniusLift_reduction`: The reduction of `σ` modulo `π` on `O_E/πO_E = k((t))` is `x ↦ x^q`.
- `frobeniusLift_ext_image`: If `σ, σ'` are Frobenius lifts with `σ_K = σ'_K` and `σ(t) = σ'(t)` then `σ = σ'` on `O_E`.
- The reduction of `σ` modulo `π` on `R^int/πR^int = k((t))` is `x ↦ x^q`.
- Analytic extension and the cyclotomic logarithm identity are checked in [§RD.0.46](#rd-0-46).

<a id="rd-0-6"></a>

### RD.0.6 Partial valuations `v_n, w_r` on Witt vectors and the overconvergent Witt vectors `W_con`

**Definition.** Let `ℓ` be a perfect field of characteristic `p` with a (possibly trivial) valuation `v_ℓ`, complete, let `k_0 ⊆ ℓ` be a perfect subfield on which `v_ℓ` is trivial, and let `O` be a finite totally ramified extension of `W(k_0)` with uniformiser `π`, equipped with an extension of `σ`; put `W(ℓ, O) = W(ℓ) ⊗_{W(k_0)} O`. Every `x ∈ W(ℓ, O)[π^{-1}]` has a unique Teichmüller expansion `x = Σ_{i∈Z} [z_i] π^i` (`z_i ∈ ℓ`, zero for `i` ≪ 0). For `n ∈ Z` put `v_n(x) = min_{i ≤ n} v_ℓ(z_i)`; for `r > 0` put `v_{n,r}(x) = r·v_n(x) + n`; at `r = 0` set `v_{n,0}(x) = n` when `v_n(x)` is finite and `∞` otherwise, let `W_r(ℓ, O)` be the set of `x ∈ W(ℓ, O)` with `v_{n,r}(x) → ∞` as `n → ∞`, and `w_r(x) = min_n v_{n,r}(x); w = w_0` is the `π`-adic valuation normalised by `w(π) = 1`. Put `W_con(ℓ, O) = ∪_{r>0} W_r(ℓ, O)`.

*Hypotheses.*

- `ℓ` perfect and complete for `v_ℓ`; the valuation may be trivial, in which case `W_r = W` and `W_con = W(ℓ, O)`.
- Normalisation `w(π) = 1` (Kedlaya, slope filtrations revisited, Remark 2.1.11), not `w(p) = 1`; results do not depend on it.
- `σ` on `W(ℓ, O)` is the `log_p(q)`-th power of the Witt vector Frobenius `σ_0`, tensored with the given `σ` on `O`; then `v_n(x^σ) = q·v_n(x)` and `w_r(x) = w_{r/q}(x^σ)`.

The API:

- `WittPartial.v`: The partial valuation `v_n(x) = min_{i ≤ n} v_ℓ(z_i)` on `W(ℓ, O)[π^{-1}]`, valued in `R ∪ {∞}`.
- `WittPartial.w`: `w_r(x) = min_n v_{n,r}(x)`; at `r = 0` use the separately defined `v_{n,0}`, so `w_0` is the `π`-adic valuation.
- `WittPartial.overconvergentSubring`: The subring `W_r(ℓ, O)` of `x` with `v_{n,r}(x) → ∞` as `n → ∞`, and `W_con = ∪_r W_r`.
- `WittPartial.v_add`: `v_n(x + y) ≥ min(v_n(x), v_n(y))`, with equality if the minimum is attained once.
- `WittPartial.v_mul`: `v_n`(xy) `≥ min_m (v_m(x) + v_{n−m}(y))`, with equality if the minimum is attained once.
- `WittPartial.v_frobenius`: `v_n(x^σ) = q·v_n(x)`; hence `w_r(x) = w_{r/q}(x^σ)`.
- `WittPartial.v_teichmuller`: `v_n([z]) = v_ℓ(z)` for `n ≥ 0` and `z ∈ ℓ`.

*Proof sketch.*

1. Existence and uniqueness of Teichmüller expansions: each `x ∈ W(ℓ, O)` is uniquely `Σ_{i≥0} [z_i] π^i` (slope filtrations revisited, Definition 2.1.4); inverting `π` allows finitely many negative `i`.
2. The inequalities `v_n(x + y) ≥ min(v_n(x), v_n(y)), v_n`(xy) `≥ min_m (v_m(x) + v_{n−m}(y))` with equality when the minimum is attained once, `v_n(x^σ) = q v_n(x)` and `v_n([z]) = v_ℓ(z)` for `n ≥ 0` follow from the Witt vector addition and multiplication formulas (Definition 2.1.5).
3. `σ` sends `W_{qr}` onto `W_r` (Definition 2.1.5); `W_r` is a subring by the inequalities.

*Sources.* Kedlaya, *Slope filtrations revisited*, Definition 2.1.4, p. 6, and Definition 2.1.5, p. 6, and Definition 2.1.8, p. 7.

*Needs:* Mathlib `WittVector`; Mathlib `WittVector.teichmuller`; Mathlib `WittVector.frobenius`; Mathlib `AddValuation`.

**Checks.**

- `wittPartial_v_teichmuller`: For `z ∈ ℓ` nonzero: `v_n([z]) = v_ℓ(z)` for all `n ≥ 0` and `v_n([z]) = ∞` for `n < 0`.
- `wittPartial_w_pi`: `w_r(π) = 1`; for `z ≠ 0, w_r([z]) = r·v_ℓ(z)` for `r ≥ 0; w_r(0) = ∞`.
- `wittPartial_trivial_valuation`: If `v_ℓ` is trivial then `W_r(ℓ, O) = W(ℓ, O)` for all `r ≥ 0` and `w_r = w`.
- `wittPartial_compat_mathlib_witt`: For `O = W(k_0)` and `π = p, W(ℓ, O)` is Mathlib's `WittVector p ℓ` and the Teichmüller lift is WittVector.teichmuller.
- `wittPartial_not_overconvergent`: If `y ∈ ℓ` has `v_ℓ(y) < 0`, the element `x = Σ_{i≥0} [y^{q^i}] π^i` of `W(ℓ, O)` satisfies `v_{n,r}(x) = r q^n v_ℓ(y) + n → −∞`, so `x` lies in no `W_r(ℓ, O)` with `r > 0`.
- For `ℓ` with trivial valuation `W_r(ℓ, O) = W(ℓ, O)` for every `r`.
- For `z ∈ ℓ` with `v_ℓ(z) > 0` the Teichmüller lift `[z]` lies in every `W_r` and is a unit in `W_r` if `z ≠ 0` (Remark 2.2.11(a)).
- If `v_ℓ(y) < 0`, then `Σ_{i≥0} [y^{q^i}] π^i` lies in `W(ℓ, O)` but in no `W_r(ℓ, O)`.

<a id="rd-0-7"></a>

### RD.0.7 `w_r` is a valuation on `W_r(ℓ, O)[π^{-1}]` (Newton-polygon additivity)

**Lemma.** For `x, y ∈ W_r(ℓ, O)[π^{-1}]` nonzero, let `i, j` be the smallest and largest `n` achieving `min_n v_{n,r}(x)`, and `k, l` those for `y`. Then `i + k` and `j + l` are the smallest and largest `n` achieving `min_n v_{n,r}`(xy), and `w_r`(xy) `= w_r(x) + w_r(y)`. In particular `w_r` is a valuation on `W_r(ℓ, O)[π^{-1}]` and `w_r(x) = w_{r/q}(x^σ)`.

*Hypotheses.* `ℓ` perfect, complete for `v_ℓ`; notation of the partial-valuation target.

*Proof sketch.* Apply `v_{m,r}`(xy) `≥ min_n (v_{n,r}(x) + v_{m−n,r}(y))` with equality when the minimum is attained once. For `m = i + k` and `m = j + l` the value `v_{i,r}(x) + v_{k,r}(y)` is attained exactly once; for `m < i + k` or `m > j + l` it is never attained; this gives the claim. (Kedlaya, *Slope filtrations revisited*, Lemma 2.1.7 and Definition 2.1.8, pp. 6-7.)

*Needs:* [§RD.0.6](#rd-0-6) *Partial valuations `v_n, w_r` on Witt vectors and the overconvergent Witt vectors `W_con`*.

**Checks.**

- Rank one check: `w_r([z]π^m) = r v_ℓ(z) + m` and the product rule holds on monomials.

<a id="rd-0-8"></a>

### RD.0.8 `W_con(ℓ, O)` is a henselian discrete valuation ring

**Lemma.** `W_con(ℓ, O)` is a discrete valuation ring with maximal ideal `(π)` and residue field `ℓ`; it is henselian, and it is not `π`-adically complete when `v_ℓ` is nontrivial.

*Hypotheses.* `ℓ` perfect and complete for `v_ℓ`.

*Proof sketch.*

1. DVR: every nonzero `x ∈ W_con` is `π^m` times an element with nonzero reduction; an element of `W_r` with nonzero reduction `u_0` is a unit in some `W_s` (Remark 2.1.10: `u` is a unit of `W_r` iff `v_{n,r}(u) > v_{0,r}(u)` for `n > 0`, which holds after shrinking `r`).
2. Henselian: given a polynomial `P` over `W_con` and `y` with `P(y) ≡ 0` and `P'(y)` ≢ 0 mod `π`, choose `r` with `w_r(P(y)/P'(y)) > 0`; Newton iteration converges both for `w` and for `w_r`, so the root lies in `W_r` (Lemma 2.1.12).
3. Non-completeness: see the non-example of the partial-valuation target.

*Sources.* Kedlaya, *Slope filtrations revisited*, Lemma 2.1.12, p. 7, and Proof of Lemma 2.1.12, p. 7.

*Needs:* [§RD.0.6](#rd-0-6) *Partial valuations `v_n, w_r` on Witt vectors and the overconvergent Witt vectors `W_con`*; [§RD.0.7](#rd-0-7) *`w_r` is a valuation on `W_r(ℓ, O)[π^{-1}]` (Newton-polygon additivity)*; Mathlib `HenselianLocalRing`; Mathlib `IsDiscreteValuationRing`.

**Checks.**

- The residue map `W_con → ℓ` is surjective (Teichmüller lifts) with kernel `πW_con`.
- Hensel test: for `p` odd and `ℓ` ∋ `y` with `y^2 = c`, the polynomial `X^2 − [c]` has a root in `W_con` lifting `y`.

<a id="rd-0-9"></a>

### RD.0.9 Kedlaya's analytic rings `Γ^ℓ_I, Γ^ℓ_an,r` and `Γ^ℓ_an,con`

**Construction.** Let `ℓ` be a field of characteristic `p` complete for a (possibly trivial) valuation `v_ℓ, k_0 ⊆ ℓ` a subfield on which `v_ℓ` is trivial, `O` finite totally ramified over the Cohen ring `C_{k_0}` with uniformiser `π, Γ = Γ^ℓ = C_ℓ ⊗_{C_{k_0}} O`, and `σ` a Frobenius lift on `Γ` (lifting the `q`-power map of `ℓ`) carrying `O` into itself. Via the completed direct limit of `Γ →σ Γ →σ ⋯ ≅ W(ℓ^perf, O^perf)` the functions `v_n, v_{n,r}, w_r` restrict to `Γ`; put `Γ_r = Γ ∩ W_r(ℓ^perf, O)`. Say `Γ` has enough `r_0`-units if every nonzero element of `ℓ` lifts to a unit of `Γ_{r_0}`, and assume this. For `I` a nonempty interval contained in [0, `r_0`) and bounded away from `r_0, Γ_I` is the Fréchet completion of `Γ_{r_0}[π^{-1}]` for the valuations `w_s, s ∈ I; Γ_an,r = Γ_`{(0,r]}, `Γ_an,con = ∪_{r<r_0} Γ_an,r, Γ_con = ∪ Γ_r` (a henselian DVR). `σ` induces `Γ_I → Γ_{q^{-1}I}`; for nonempty intervals `I ⊆ J` the restriction `Γ_J → Γ_I` is injective with dense image. The Newton polygon of `x ∈ Γ_I` is the lower convex hull of the points `(v_n(x), n)` with the segments of slope `−s, s ∉ I`, removed; its slopes (with multiplicities) are the slopes of `x`.

*Hypotheses.*

- `ℓ` complete; 'enough `r_0`-units' holds for `ℓ` perfect (Teichmüller lifts) and for `ℓ = k((t))` by the comparison of naive and true valuations (see the Robba ring comparison target) and it passes to finite separable extensions.
- When `v_ℓ` is trivial, `Γ_an,con = Γ_con[π^{-1}] = Γ[π^{-1}]` is a complete discretely valued field.
- Kedlaya's `K` is written `ℓ` here, to keep `K` for the characteristic-0 coefficient field.

The API:

- `AnalyticRing.intervalRing`: `Γ_I` for a nonempty interval `I ⊆ [`0, `r_0`) bounded away from `r_0`: the Fréchet completion of `Γ_{r_0}[π^{-1}]` for `(w_s)_{s∈I}`.
- `AnalyticRing.analyticRing`: `Γ_an,r = Γ_`{(0,r]} and `Γ_an,con = ∪_{r} Γ_an,r`, with its limit-of-Fréchet topology.
- `AnalyticRing.boundedSubring`: `Γ_con = ∪_r Γ_r`, a henselian DVR with residue field `ℓ`, and `Γ_con[π^{-1}] ⊆ Γ_an,con`.
- `AnalyticRing.restrict`: For nonempty intervals `I ⊆ J ⊆ [`0,r`_0`) bounded away from `r_0`, the injective restriction `Γ_J → Γ_I` with dense image.
- `AnalyticRing.frobenius`: `σ: Γ_I → Γ_{q^{-1}I}`, compatible with restriction.
- `AnalyticRing.slopes`: The Newton polygon and slope multiset of `x ∈ Γ_I` (slopes in `I`, finite multiplicity; for `x ∈ Γ_an,r` the slopes decrease to 0).
- `AnalyticRing.isDomain`: `Γ_I` and `Γ_an,con` are integral domains.
- `AnalyticRing.trivialValuation`: If `v_ℓ` is trivial then `Γ_an,con = Γ[π^{-1}]`.

Every `Γ_I` below has `I` a nonempty interval in [0,r`_0`), bounded away from `r_0`; the same condition applies to `J` and to every intersection used as a radius set. Singleton intervals are allowed. The empty radius set has no `Γ_I` carrier in this interface.

*Proof sketch.*

1. Definitions 2.2.1-2.2.13 of slope filtrations revisited: Cohen ring, Frobenius lift, embedding into `W(ℓ^perf, O^perf), Γ_r`, enough units, `Γ_con`.
2. Definition 2.4.2: Fréchet completion `Γ_I`; the functions `v_n, v_{n,s}, w_s` extend by continuity; `σ: Γ_I → Γ_{q^{-1}I}`; restriction maps injective with dense image (density of `Γ_{r_0}[π^{-1}]`).
3. Definition 2.4.4 (Newton polygon of elements) and Definition 2.4.8 `(Γ_an,con)`.
4. `Γ_con` is a henselian DVR with residue field `ℓ`: Definition 2.2.13 with Lemma 2.1.12 applied inside `W_con(ℓ^perf, O)`.

*Sources.* Kedlaya, *Slope filtrations revisited*, Definition 2.2.3, p. 8, and Definition 2.2.10, p. 8, and Definition 2.4.2, p. 14, and Definition 2.4.8, p. 15.

*Needs:* [§RD.0.6](#rd-0-6) *Partial valuations `v_n, w_r` on Witt vectors and the overconvergent Witt vectors `W_con`*; [§RD.0.7](#rd-0-7) *`w_r` is a valuation on `W_r(ℓ, O)[π^{-1}]` (Newton-polygon additivity)*; [§RD.0.8](#rd-0-8) *`W_con(ℓ, O)` is a henselian discrete valuation ring*.

**Checks.**

- `analyticRing_trivial_valuation`: If `v_ℓ` is trivial, `Γ_an,con = Γ[π^{-1}]` and every nonzero element is a unit.
- `analyticRing_closed_interval`: For `I = [0, s], Γ_I = Γ_s[π^{-1}]`.
- `analyticRing_slopes_monomial`: For `ℓ = k((t)), O = W(k)` and the standard lift, the Laurent polynomial `t − p` has exactly one slope, equal to 1 with multiplicity 1 (its zero lies on `|t| = |π|^1`), while `u·π^m` for a unit `u` of `Γ_{r_0}` has no slopes.
- `analyticRing_compat_robba`: For `ℓ = k((t))` and a Frobenius lift with `σ(t)` overconvergent, `Γ_an,con` coincides with the Robba ring constructed in the Frobenius-lift target (see the comparison target).
- `analyticRing_not_noetherian`: For `ℓ = k((t))` in mixed characteristic, put `f_j = ∏_{i≥2, 2^j ∣ i}(1 − t^(p^i)/p^i)` for `j ≥ 0`. These products converge uniformly on every closed disc of radius less than 1, since `|p|^(−i) ρ^(p^i) → 0`, and define nonzero Robba elements. Write `f_j = g_j f_(j+1)`, where `g_j` is the product over `i ≥ 2` with `2^j ∣ i` and `2^(j+1) ∤ i`. Then `(f_j) ⊊ (f_(j+1))` even as annular germs: the zeros of `g_j` have distinct radii `|p|^(i/p^i) → 1` and `f_(j+1)` is nonzero at those zeros. On every sufficiently thin annulus, evaluating a putative identity `f_(j+1) = h f_j` at such a zero is impossible. Hence `⋃_j (f_j)` is not finitely generated.
- For comparison, the tails `x_j = ∏_{i≥j}(1 − t^(p^i)/p^i)` are associated as Robba germs: their consecutive quotient is a polynomial whose roots all have radius `|p|^(j/p^j) < 1`, and is a unit on a thinner annulus. Thus their ideals are equal, whereas each quotient `g_j` above has zeros in every boundary annulus.
- For `ℓ` with trivial valuation: `Γ_I = Γ[π^{-1}]` for every `I` and `Γ_an,con = Γ[π^{-1}]`.
- For `ℓ = k((t)): Γ_an,con` is the Robba ring (comparison target).

- The empty set is excluded: completing for no seminorms gives the zero separated ring, so it cannot support the domain or injective-restriction assertions.

<a id="rd-0-10"></a>

### RD.0.10 Slopes of a product are the sums of the slopes; `Γ_I` is a domain

**Lemma.** For `x, y ∈ Γ_I` nonzero and `s ∈ I`, the multiplicity of `s` as a slope of xy is the sum of its multiplicities as a slope of `x` and of `y`. In particular `Γ_I` and `Γ_an,con` are integral domains. For a closed interval `[r', r] ⊆ [`0, `r_0`) the total multiplicity of `x ∈ Γ_{[r',r]}` is finite and equals `i − j`, where `i` is the largest `n` achieving `min_n v_{n,r}(x)` and `j` the smallest `n` achieving `min_n v_{n,r'}(x)`.

*Hypotheses.* Notation of the analytic-ring construction.

*Proof sketch.*

1. For `x, y ∈ Γ_r[π^{-1}]` this is the multiplicativity lemma for `w_r` applied at each `s ∈ I`.
2. In general approximate `x, y` in `Γ_I` by elements of `Γ_r[π^{-1}]` closely enough that the extremal indices are unchanged (Lemma 2.4.7).
3. Finiteness of total multiplicity: Remark 2.4.6.

*Sources.* Kedlaya, *Slope filtrations revisited*, Lemma 2.4.7, p. 15, and Remark 2.4.6, p. 15.

*Needs:* [§RD.0.9](#rd-0-9) *Kedlaya's analytic rings `Γ^ℓ_I, Γ^ℓ_an,r` and `Γ^ℓ_an,con`*; [§RD.0.7](#rd-0-7) *`w_r` is a valuation on `W_r(ℓ, O)[π^{-1}]` (Newton-polygon additivity)*.

**Checks.**

- For elements of `O[π^{-1}]^×` there are no slopes; a product of two elements each with one slope `s` of multiplicity 1 has slope `s` with multiplicity 2.

<a id="rd-0-11"></a>

### RD.0.11 Semiunit presentations of elements of `Γ_I`

**Lemma.** Call a semiunit an element of `Γ_{r_0}` that is zero or a unit. For `I` a nonempty interval contained in [0, `r_0`) and bounded away from `r_0`, every `x ∈ Γ_I` admits a semiunit presentation `x = Σ_{i∈Z} u_i π^i` (`u_i` semiunits, the sum converging in `Γ_I`). For any semiunits `u_i` and `r ∈ (0, r_0), w_r(u_i π^i) ≥ min_{n≤i} v_{n,r}(Σ_{j≤i} u_j π^j)`.

*Hypotheses.* `Γ` has enough `r_0`-units (this is what makes each residue class liftable to a semiunit).

*Proof sketch.*

1. Lemma 2.5.3(a),(b): estimates for partial sums of semiunit series, by induction on `i`.
2. Lemma 2.5.4: a semiunit presentation over `Γ_{[r,r]}` of an element with `v_{n,s}(x) → ∞` for `s ∈ I` converges in `Γ_I`.
3. Proposition 2.5.5: first for `x ∈ Γ_r` by successive `π`-adic approximation with semiunits; then for `I = [`r,r] by approximating `x` by elements `x_l ∈ Γ_r[π^{-1}]` and correcting finitely many terms at each stage; the corrections for a fixed `i` form a series converging in `Γ_{r_0}` whose limit is a semiunit; the general `I` follows from Lemma 2.5.4.

*Sources.* Kedlaya, *Slope filtrations revisited*, Definition 2.5.2 and Proposition 2.5.5, pp. 16-18.

*Needs:* [§RD.0.9](#rd-0-9) *Kedlaya's analytic rings `Γ^ℓ_I, Γ^ℓ_an,r` and `Γ^ℓ_an,con`*; [§RD.0.10](#rd-0-10) *Slopes of a product are the sums of the slopes; `Γ_I` is a domain*.

**Checks.**

- If `ℓ` is perfect, the Teichmüller presentation `Σ [f_n(x)] π^n` is a semiunit presentation.

- A finite sum of semiunits times powers of `π` gives a presentation on every allowed `I` on which its coefficients are defined.
- For `x=1` the presentation `u_0=1` and `u_i=0` for `i≠0` works on a singleton interval; `I=∅` is outside the contract.

<a id="rd-0-12"></a>

### RD.0.12 Numerical membership criterion, intersections and Mayer-Vietoris splitting for `Γ_I`

**Lemma.** (a) For `r ∈ (0, r_0)` and `x ∈ Γ_{[r,r]}: x ∈ Γ_r` iff `v_n(x) = ∞` for all `n < 0`. (b) For nonempty intervals `I ⊆ J ⊆ [`0,r`_0`) bounded away from `r_0` and `x ∈ Γ_I` with `v_{n,s}(x) → ∞` as `n → ±∞` for every `s ∈ J: x ∈ Γ_J`. (c) For `ℓ ⊆ ℓ'` complete, `Γ^ℓ` and `Γ^{ℓ'}` having enough `r_0`-units, and nonempty intervals `I ⊆ J ⊆ [`0, `r_0`) bounded away from `r_0: Γ^ℓ_I ∩ Γ^{ℓ'}_J = Γ^ℓ_J` inside `Γ^{ℓ'}_I`; in particular `Γ^ℓ[π^{-1}] ∩ Γ^{ℓ'}_con[π^{-1}] = Γ^ℓ_con[π^{-1}]`. (d) For `I = [`a,b], `J = [`c,d] with `0 ≤ a ≤ c ≤ b ≤ d < r_0: Γ_I ∩ Γ_J = Γ_{I∪J}` inside `Γ_{I∩J}`, and every `x ∈ Γ_{I∩J}` with `w_s(x) > 0` on `I∩J` splits as `y + z, y ∈ Γ_I, z ∈ Γ_J`, with `w_s(y) ≥ (s/c)w_c(x)` on [a,c] when `c>0, w_s(z) ≥ (s/b)w_b(x)` on [b,d] when `b>0, min(w_s(y), w_s(z)) ≥ w_s(x)` on [c,b]. (e) For `I` a nonempty closed interval ⊆ [0,r] and `x ∈ Γ_I`, assume `r ∈ I` or that `min_{n<0} v_{n,s}(x)` is finite for every `s ∈ I`. Then there is `y ∈ Γ_r` with `w_s(x − y) ≥ min_{n<0} v_{n,s}(x)` for `s ∈ I`.

*Hypotheses.* Enough `r_0`-units for all rings involved.

*Proof sketch.*

1. (a) Corollary 2.5.6 from a semiunit presentation: a nonzero `u_j, j < 0`, would give `v_{j}(x) < ∞`.
2. (b) Corollary 2.5.7: take a semiunit presentation over `Γ_I` and apply Lemma 2.5.4.
3. (c) Corollary 2.5.8 from (b); the special case with `I = [0,0]` and `J = [`0,s], `s → 0`, gives the intersection statement used in the comparison of generic and special polygons.
4. (d) Corollary 2.5.9: split a semiunit presentation into the parts with `i ≤ 0` and `i > 0`.
5. (e) Lemma 2.5.11: truncate a semiunit presentation.

*Sources.* Kedlaya, *Slope filtrations revisited*, Corollary 2.5.6, p. 18, and Corollary 2.5.8, p. 19, and Corollary 2.5.9, p. 19, and Proof of Theorem 5.5.2, p. 59.

*Needs:* [§RD.0.11](#rd-0-11) *Semiunit presentations of elements of `Γ_I`*.

**Checks.**

- For `ℓ=k((t))` with the standard Laurent lift, `x=t⁻¹` lies in `Γ_r` and has `v_n(x)=∞` for all `n<0`, whereas `x=π⁻¹` does not satisfy this condition. The criterion tests integrality in the `π`-expansion, not absence of negative `t`-powers.

- For `I=J=[`r,r] with `0<r<r_0` the intersection identity is the identity on `Γ_{[r,r]}`.
- For `0<a<c<b<d<r_0`, restrictions from `Γ_{[a,d]}` into `Γ_{[c,b]}` agree through either overlapping interval. The disjoint case `b<c` has no `Γ_{I∩J}` carrier.

<a id="rd-0-13"></a>

### RD.0.13 Units of `Γ_I` are the elements without slopes; units of `Γ_an,r` lie in `Γ_r[π^{-1}]`

**Theorem.** A nonzero `x ∈ Γ_I` is a unit of `Γ_I` iff it has no slopes (in `I`). If `I =` (0, `r]`, this holds iff `x` is a unit of `Γ_r[π^{-1}]`. Consequently the units of `Γ_an,con` are exactly the units of `Γ_con[π^{-1}]`, i.e. the nonzero elements of the field `Γ_con[π^{-1}]`.

*Hypotheses.*

- Enough `r_0`-units.
- `Γ_con` is a DVR, so `Γ_con[π^{-1}]` is its fraction field.

*Proof sketch.*

1. Units have no slopes by slope additivity.
2. Conversely if `x` has no slopes, one `index m` minimises `v_{m,s}(x)` for all `s ∈ I`; normalise `m = 0`; the truncation lemma (e) gives `y ∈ Γ_r` close to `x`, and enough units gives a unit `z` of `Γ_r` with `w(y − z) > 0`; then `w_s(1 − x z^{-1}) > 0` on `I` and `Σ (1 − x z^{-1})^i` converges to `(x z^{-1})^{-1}`.
3. For `I =` (0, `r]`: no slopes forces `v_n(x) = ∞` for `n < m`, so `x ∈ Γ_r[π^{-1}]` by the membership criterion, and likewise `x^{-1}`.

*Sources.* Kedlaya, *Slope filtrations revisited*, Corollary 2.5.12, p. 19.

*Needs:* [§RD.0.10](#rd-0-10) *Slopes of a product are the sums of the slopes; `Γ_I` is a domain*; [§RD.0.11](#rd-0-11) *Semiunit presentations of elements of `Γ_I`*; [§RD.0.12](#rd-0-12) *Numerical membership criterion, intersections and Mayer-Vietoris splitting for `Γ_I`*.

**Checks.**

- `π` and the units of `O` are units; for `ℓ = k((t))` the element `Π_{i≥1}(1 − t^{p^i}/p^i)` of `R` has infinitely many slopes and is not a unit (monodromy paper, Section 2.3).

<a id="rd-0-14"></a>

### RD.0.14 `Γ_r` and `Γ_I` for closed `I` are principal ideal domains (Lazard)

**Theorem.** For `r ∈ (0, r_0), Γ_r` is a principal ideal domain, and for every nonempty closed interval `I ⊆ [`0, `r_0`), `Γ_I` is a principal ideal domain. For `ℓ = k((t))`, `Γ_r` is the integral-coefficient subring of the bounded analytic functions on `|π|^r ≤ |t| < 1`; inverting `π` gives all bounded functions there. For closed `I=[s,r]` with `0<s≤r`, `Γ_I` is the analytic function ring of the closed annulus `{log_{|π|}|t| ∈ I}`, giving Lazard's theorem. At `I=[0,r]` with `r>0`, `Γ_I=Γ_r[1/π]` has the bounded half-open-annulus interpretation; `Γ_{[0,0]}=E` is the Amice field.

*Hypotheses.*

- `O` is a complete discretely valued coefficient ring with uniformiser `π`; the valuation on `ℓ` need not be discrete.
- Enough `r_0`-units.

*Proof sketch.*

1. Positioning (Lemma 2.6.1): for `x ∈ Γ_{[r,r]}` nonzero there are a unit `u` of `Γ_{r_0}` and `i` with `uπ^i x` normalised (`w_r = 0, v_0(· − 1) > 0, v_{n,r} > 0` for `n < 0`).
2. Division algorithm (Lemma 2.6.3): define the height of `x ∈ Γ_r`; for `x ≠ 0` and `y` there is `z` of smaller height with `y − z ∈ xΓ_r` and `w_r(z) ≥ w_r(y)`; use a positive contraction bound on each closed subinterval and induct over the finite set of critical valuation indices, as in the corrected proof of Lemma 2.6.3.
3. `Γ_r` is a PID (Proposition 2.6.5): an element of minimal height generates any nonzero ideal.
4. Factorisation (Lemma 2.6.7): for `I = [r', r]` and `x ∈ Γ_I` there is a unit `u` of `Γ_I` with ux `∈ Γ_r` having all slopes in `I`.
5. `Γ_I` is a PID (Proposition 2.6.8): the ideal of `Γ_r` generated by the ux, `x ∈ J`, is principal by Proposition 2.6.5 (the printed proof cites 2.6.8 itself; see *Corrections to the sources*) and its generator generates `J`.

*Sources.* Kedlaya, *Slope filtrations revisited*, Proposition 2.6.5, p. 21, and Proposition 2.6.8, p. 22, and Remark 2.6.4, p. 21; Definition 2.4.2, p. 14; Kedlaya, *Local monodromy of p-adic differential equations: an overview*, Proposition 3.2.3, p. 11.
